content.text: A signed JWT is three Base64url-encoded parts joined by dots. The signature proves who issued the token and that nobody changed it, but anyone who holds the token can read every claim, no key needed. Treat the payload as public: keep personal and internal data on the server, and use encryption (JWE) only when claims must travel privately to another party.

A tester files a bug: the access token the app keeps in local storage contains her test customer's email, phone number, date of birth and credit limit. A developer closes it as "not a bug", because the token is encrypted. She pastes it into a decoder and reads all of it back. No key, no password: the token was never encrypted, only signed.
The common misconception
The belief: a JWT is encrypted, so it's safe to put sensitive data in its payload. Only the server, which holds the key, can read it.

It's easy to believe because nothing about a token looks readable. It's a long run of random-looking characters, it's produced by a security library with a "signing key", and the server rejects it if anything is off. The spec adds to the confusion: RFC 7519 says JWT claims can be "digitally signed or integrity protected with a Message Authentication Code (MAC) and/or encrypted." So JWTs can be encrypted. But in what OWASP calls "its most common form", a JWT is only signed, and signing and encrypting are different jobs.
What actually happens
A signed JWT is three Base64url parts
OWASP's JSON Web Token Cheat Sheet shows the structure of a signed
JWT
in one line:
{base64url(json(header))}.{base64url(json(claims))}.{base64url(signature)}
. That's the JWS compact serialization from RFC 7515. The header and the claims are plain JSON, run through
Base64
url so they're safe in URLs and headers. The
eyJ
that starts almost every token is just how Base64 begins
, the opening of a JSON object.
The signature protects integrity, not secrecy

RFC 7515 describes a JWS as "content secured with digital signatures or Message Authentication Codes (MACs)." A signature lets the server check two things: the token came from someone holding the key, and not one byte has changed. OWASP draws the line clearly: a signed JWT "provides integrity and authenticity, but not confidentiality. The payload is only base64url encoded, not encrypted, so anyone who obtains the token can read every claim."
HTTPS doesn't keep the claims private either

TLS protects the token on the wire, and that's all. OWASP lists where the claims stay exposed: "in application logs, in browser storage, in referrer headers, and to any intermediary that terminates TLS." Add every script running on your page, and anyone the token is accidentally shared with. A JWT access token is also a
bearer credential
: whoever holds it can use it until it expires.
Encryption is a different format: JWE
When claims really must be secret, the spec has
JWE

. RFC 7516 says it "represents encrypted content", and its compact form has five parts, not three: a protected header, an encrypted key, an initialization vector, the ciphertext and an authentication tag. JWE alone doesn't prove who issued the token, so OWASP recommends signing first and encrypting the result. Its first advice, though, is simpler: "Prefer keeping sensitive data server-side behind an opaque reference token."

Access and ID tokens with few claims
Claims a third party must read privately

blocks.title: Reading a token isn't verifying it

content.text: Decoding is fine for showing a name in the UI, never for a security decision. RFC 8725 recounts attacks where the
alg
header was changed to
none
"and some libraries would trust this value". On the server, validate the signature with a fixed list of algorithms, then check issuer, audience and expiry.

blocks.title: Anyone with a token can attack a weak HS256 key

content.text: Because tokens are readable and easy to get, a weak shared secret is a real risk. RFC 8725 warns that keys "with insufficient entropy (such as a human-memorable password)" are "vulnerable to offline brute-force or dictionary attacks once an attacker gets hold of such a token." Generate the key from a secure random source.
Add a test that issues a token, decodes the payload and fails if any claim falls outside an allow-list such as
sub
iss
aud
exp
iat
nbf
and
scope
. New claims then need a deliberate decision.
How to apply it in your project

items.title: Decode the tokens you issue today

content.text: Take an access token and an ID token from a test account, decode them, and list every claim. Assume anyone who sees the token can read the same list.

items.title: Cut the payload to what authorization needs

content.text: Keep a stable, non-personal user ID in
sub
, plus
iss
aud
exp
and any scopes or roles the API checks. Remove personal data and internal business values.

items.title: Look up the rest on the server

content.text: Fetch profile and account data by
sub
when a request needs it, or use opaque reference tokens, as OWASP prefers, for sessions that carry sensitive context.

items.title: Use JWE only for claims that must travel

content.text: If another party must read private claims and can't ask your server, sign the token and then encrypt it as a JWE. Validate both layers on the receiving side.
Pin the accepted algorithms, use a long random key for HS256 or an asymmetric key pair, and check issuer, audience and expiry on every request.
Key takeaways

items.text: A signed JWT is Base64url-encoded JSON plus a signature; anyone can read its claims.
The signature proves who issued the token and that it wasn't changed; it hides nothing.
HTTPS protects the token in transit only; logs, browser storage and scripts can still read it.
Keep personal and business data out of the payload; look it up on the server by
Use JWE, signed then encrypted, only when private claims must travel to another party.
